rv.q: As embodied by these two high-caliber performances, Coble creates a thoughtful, potentially enriching gift to the audience.

In these moments, and in Ms. Parsons’s more than capable hands, Mr. Coble’s play rises above its slightly formulaic structure to become a dry-eyed, moving rumination on the hard fact that the progress of human life being what it is, truly happy endings are rare indeed.
It's a feeble, contrived conceit, albeit one dealing with substantial and sadly relevant issues about the indignities of aging.
Wonderful performances by the two stars compensate for the contrivances of this schematic comedy-drama.
Both actors are perfectly fine, but watching them duke it out is only mildly entertaining — the play’s brushstrokes are too broad to paint a compelling portrait.
Even with actors the caliber of Parsons and Spinella, however, this is a once-over-lightly insult to a subject that deserves so much more than a mechanical showcase for gold-standard performers.

The play offers no groundbreaking revelations about the nature of these complex familial dynamics and obligations — nor about our captivity on this endlessly revolving carousel of time (to borrow from Joni Mitchell).
Ironically, the dominant sensation produced by Eric Coble’s anemic two-hander is also that of growing old.
This new Broadway production is ridiculous not just on the copyright page of the script by Eric Coble but also on every page thereafter.
Both performances are engaging enough to power through what's otherwise well-worn terrain.

The play itself, however, feels over written.
Kirk Lynn is an intriguing, promising and wise playwright.

Eric Coble's 90-minute two-character comedy 'The Velocity of Autumn,' which has arrived on Broadway as a star vehicle for 86-year-old Oscar winner Estelle Parsons and two-time Tony winner Stephen Spinella, is the sort of well-meaning but static and underwhelming play that would be better suited for a budget-conscious regional theater...
Too bad their vehicle is so rickety.
But this play elicits a definite response: avoid.

cn.t: Parsons earns praise for her spirited performance, but critics find Coble's two-hander about an elderly woman's defiant stand against aging schematic and underwhelming, with most dismissing it as sitcom-level material better suited for regional theater.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
